sections.h2: Where is Cheyenne and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Cheyenne is the capital of Wyoming and the county seat of Laramie County, in the far southeast corner of the state. It sits at about 6,086 feet above sea level on Crow Creek and Dry Creek, and covers a little over 32 square miles.

Two interstates meet southwest of town. I-25 runs north to south and I-80 runs east to west, and I-180 loops through the city along US 85. Cheyenne Regional Airport offers daily nonstop United Express flights to Denver, and local buses run through the Cheyenne Transit Program. A seller here is rarely more than a few minutes from a major road, which matters when a buyer asks about commute times.

The city has several historic districts, and homes inside them may face extra review:

  • Downtown Cheyenne Historic District
  • Lakeview Historic District
  • Rainsford Historic District
  • Capitol North Historic District
  • South Side Historic District

If your house sits inside one of these areas, ask the city's Planning and Development office what applies before you spend money on repairs.

sections.h2: What is the short history of Cheyenne?
sections.html:
The Union Pacific Railroad platted Cheyenne on July 5, 1867, and the first train rolled in on November 14 of that year. The city has been Wyoming's only capital since it was named the temporary territorial capital on May 7, 1869.

Fort D. A. Russell was founded in September 1867 and later became Francis E. Warren Air Force Base in October 1949. That base is one of the oldest continuously active military installations in the country, and it still shapes the housing market through transfers and deployments.

Wyoming became a state on July 10, 1890.

Government, transportation, the military and a growing technology sector carry the Cheyenne economy. State offices, Union Pacific and BNSF rail yards, and F.E. Warren Air Force Base are long-standing anchors.

Newer names have joined them. Wyoming's business council lists Microsoft, Meta, Magpul, Searing Industries and Eagle Claw as major employers, and reports combined data center investment from Meta and Microsoft of more than $1.8 billion. Cheyenne Regional, the local hospital, reports more than 2,000 employees, and a Veterans Affairs medical center also serves the area.

sections.h2: How does Cheyenne's weather affect a house?
sections.html:
Cheyenne is cold and semiarid, with strong summer thunderstorms, and hail is the weather that does the most harm to a roof. The National Weather Service reports that Cheyenne sees more than 6 days a year with severe hail of an inch or larger nearby, with June the busiest month and July next.

Quarter-size hail is the most commonly reported size. Hail can fall anywhere from March into October, and most reports come late in the afternoon.

The city's own climate numbers are worth knowing too:

  • Average annual precipitation is about 15.9 inches, mostly from May through August.
  • Seasonal snowfall averages about 60 inches, with March and April the snowiest months.
  • Lows reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit on roughly nine mornings a year.
  • The growing season runs about 106 days.

For a seller, this means buyers and inspectors will look closely at shingles, gutters, siding and furnace age. A roof with visible hail bruising can lower an offer or stall a financed sale. A cash buyer who purchases as-is does not ask you to fix that first.

sections.h2: Is flood risk a concern when selling in Cheyenne?
sections.html:
Flood risk is a real topic in Cheyenne because of the flash flood of August 1, 1985. The National Weather Service recorded 6.06 inches of rain in about three hours, 12 deaths, 70 injuries and more than $61 million in damage.

After the flood, a FEMA report called for better stormwater and floodplain management, and the city adopted new drainage plans and retention projects in the late 1980s. Today the city's Engineering Services Department keeps flood insurance rate maps and base flood elevations. You can reach it at 2101 O'Neil Ave., Room 206, or by phone at (307) 637-6268.

If your home is near Crow Creek or Dry Creek, check the map before you list. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance, and finding that out late can cost you days.

sections.h2: Which Cheyenne permits and code rules matter before a sale?
sections.html:
The City of Cheyenne requires a permit for many repairs sellers consider, including reroofing, decks, garages, water heaters, and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Permit review can take up to 10 business days, and fees are based on project value.

Some smaller jobs are exempt. A detached shed under 200 square feet needs no permit, and flatwork such as a concrete patio generally does not, unless it is in the city right-of-way. Fences over 6 feet need a permit, and the city limits fences to 4 feet in front of the house.

  • Carports over 200 square feet, or attached to another structure, need a permit.
  • Zoning violations can carry fines of $100 per day.
  • Structures built in a setback may have to be removed.

Cheyenne treats short-term rentals like other residential uses, so there is no separate registration, but each rental must hold the approvals it needs. If you have an unpermitted deck, shed or carport, call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 before a buyer finds it in an inspection.

sections.h2: When are Laramie County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Laramie County property taxes are due in two halves, with the first half payable by November 10 and the second half payable by May 10 of the following year. If you pay the whole bill by December 31, interest on the first half is waived.

Taxes not paid by the payable date become delinquent, and delinquent taxes accrue interest at 18 percent per year. If a bill is still unpaid on May 11, the treasurer certifies a delinquent list, and the county holds a lien that can lead to a tax sale. The Laramie County Treasurer is at 309 W. 20th Street, Cheyenne.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1. If you bought or recorded a deed after that date, the notice may not carry your name, but you are still responsible for the tax. The assessor mails schedules no later than the fourth Monday in April, and you have 30 days from the mailing to file a written objection. Our Wyoming property tax guide covers appeals in more detail.

sections.h2: What happens at closing and recording in Cheyenne?
sections.html:
A deed for a Cheyenne sale is recorded with the Laramie County Clerk, and the clerk cannot accept it until a sworn statement of the price and terms is filed. Wyoming law, W.S. 34-1-142, makes that statement confidential, so the sale price does not become a public record.

The clerk's recording fee is $12 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, and documents with several legal descriptions carry an added $15.50 administrative fee. The office is at 309 W 20th St, Suite 1600, and takes e-recording through several vendors. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Cheyenne homeowner?
sections.html:
A cash sale means a buyer purchases your house without a lender, so the deal does not depend on an appraisal or loan approval. You tell us about the property, we review it, and you decide whether the offer works for you.

This route often suits sellers who face one of these situations:

  • An inherited house that needs probate paperwork and cleanout.
  • A hail-damaged roof or older systems that would fail a lender's inspection.
  • A military or job move with a fixed date.
  • Back taxes or a payment problem that is getting worse.

We buy as-is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer. Call or text (424) 435-2326 or use the form on this page to start.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell my house in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close faster than a listing because it skips lender approval and appraisal. The exact timeline depends on title work, any probate, and the date you choose. Tell us your deadline and we will work around it.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix hail damage before selling in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: No, not if you sell to a cash buyer who purchases as-is. If you list on the open market, a hail-damaged roof often comes up in the inspection and can lower the offer or require repairs. Note that reroofing needs a City of Cheyenne permit.

faqs.q: Is my sale price public in Wyoming?
faqs.a: No. The sworn statement of consideration filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142 and is not a public record. The county uses it for statistical purposes.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Laramie County?
faqs.a: Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Interest on the first half is waived if you pay the full bill by December 31, and delinquent taxes accrue 18 percent interest per year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a permit or a flood map in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: Call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 for permits and Engineering Services at (307) 637-6268 for flood maps and base flood elevations. Planning and Development at (307) 637-6282 handles zoning, fences and setbacks.
